output.name: Tessan
output.myth: Ennu the Kite-Wright made the first black-tailed kite from old sailcloth and a hank of ewe's wool dyed in soot. Nobody asked him why. He said grief is heavy and wants something to hold it down. So on the morning after a death, the family climbs to the cliff edge and ties the black tail to the cord, so the dead can see the way up to Vel. Hirun the gull watches from the north-east, wet and bent-footed, and carries the count up to Hesk at the pole. Hesk counts every one as it climbs, knot by knot, the way the Tally Kite counts for her. Tavo the Gale once tore a black kite from a widow's hands and laughed until the rocks rang, and she let it go. Aun flew the first one he was sorry for, and it went up and never came down. Kessal the Knife-Beak sits in the north-west and remembers the shore birds' lost string. Our hands are still on the string, and the wool still smells of smoke. Fly it at dawn. Vel is not far, only cold.
output.finding: Start at Hirun, the bright gull star to the north-east, and Tessan lies a fist and a bit to its south-west.
